claim: Solar ultraviolet radiation (UVR) is a major source of skin damage, resulting in inflammation, premature ageing, and cancer.
source: Solar ultraviolet radiation (UVR) is a major source of skin damage, resulting in inflammation, premature ageing, and cancer.
evidence: This is a general statement about UVR effects that draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: Acute and chronic UVR exposure led to selective loss of fibroblasts from the upper dermis in human and mouse skin.
source: We show that acute and chronic UVR exposure led to selective loss of fibroblasts from the upper dermis in human and mouse skin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript including immunofluorescence quantification.

claim: Repair following acute UVR is predominantly mediated by papillary fibroblast proliferation.
source: Lineage tracing and in vivo live imaging revealed that repair following acute UVR is predominantly mediated by papillary fibroblast proliferation and fibroblast reorganisation occurs with minimal migration.
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing experiments and live imaging data shown in the manuscript.

claim: Fibroblast reorganisation occurs with minimal migration following acute UVR.
source: Lineage tracing and in vivo live imaging revealed that repair following acute UVR is predominantly mediated by papillary fibroblast proliferation and fibroblast reorganisation occurs with minimal migration.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo live imaging experiments tracking fibroblast movement.

claim: Chronic UVR exposure led to a permanent loss of papillary fibroblasts.
source: In contrast, chronic UVR exposure led to a permanent loss of papillary fibroblasts, with expansion of fibroblast membrane protrusions partially compensating for the reduction in cell number.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of fibroblast density over time after chronic UVR treatment.

claim: Expansion of fibroblast membrane protrusions partially compensates for the reduction in cell number after chronic UVR.
source: In contrast, chronic UVR exposure led to a permanent loss of papillary fibroblasts, with expansion of fibroblast membrane protrusions partially compensating for the reduction in cell number.
evidence: This is supported by measurements of fibroblast cell elongation in lineage-traced skin.

claim: UVR strongly activated Wnt signalling in skin.
source: Although UVR strongly activated Wnt signalling in skin, stimulation of fibroblast proliferation by epidermal β-catenin stabilisation did not enhance papillary dermis repair.
evidence: This is supported by TOPEGFP reporter mouse data showing increased Wnt activity.

claim: Stimulation of fibroblast proliferation by epidermal β-catenin stabilisation did not enhance papillary dermis repair.
source: Although UVR strongly activated Wnt signalling in skin, stimulation of fibroblast proliferation by epidermal β-catenin stabilisation did not enhance papillary dermis repair.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using Krt14ΔNβ-cat transgenic mice.

claim: Acute UVR triggered an infiltrate of neutrophils and T cell subpopulations.
source: Acute UVR triggered an infiltrate of neutrophils and T cell subpopulations and increased pro-inflammatory prostaglandin signalling in skin.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and flow cytometry data showing immune cell infiltration.

claim: Acute UVR increased pro-inflammatory prostaglandin signalling in skin.
source: Acute UVR triggered an infiltrate of neutrophils and T cell subpopulations and increased pro-inflammatory prostaglandin signalling in skin.
evidence: This is supported by PGE-2 measurements in skin samples.

claim: Depletion of CD4- and CD8-positive cells resulted in increased papillary fibroblast depletion.
source: Depletion of CD4- and CD8-positive cells resulted in increased papillary fibroblast depletion, which correlated with an increase in DNA damage, pro-inflammatory prostaglandins, and reduction in fibroblast proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by antibody depletion experiments with quantification of fibroblast density.

claim: CD4 and CD8 cell depletion correlated with an increase in DNA damage in fibroblasts.
source: Depletion of CD4- and CD8-positive cells resulted in increased papillary fibroblast depletion, which correlated with an increase in DNA damage, pro-inflammatory prostaglandins, and reduction in fibroblast proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by yH2AX staining quantification in T cell depleted mice.

claim: CD4 and CD8 cell depletion correlated with an increase in pro-inflammatory prostaglandins.
source: Depletion of CD4- and CD8-positive cells resulted in increased papillary fibroblast depletion, which correlated with an increase in DNA damage, pro-inflammatory prostaglandins, and reduction in fibroblast proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by PGE-2 measurements after T cell depletion.

claim: CD4 and CD8 cell depletion correlated with reduction in fibroblast proliferation.
source: Depletion of CD4- and CD8-positive cells resulted in increased papillary fibroblast depletion, which correlated with an increase in DNA damage, pro-inflammatory prostaglandins, and reduction in fibroblast proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by Ki67 staining quantification in T cell depleted mice.

claim: Topical COX-2 inhibition prevented fibroblast depletion after UVR.
source: Conversely, topical COX-2 inhibition prevented fibroblast depletion and neutrophil infiltration after UVR.
evidence: This is supported by celecoxib treatment experiments with fibroblast density quantification.

claim: Topical COX-2 inhibition prevented neutrophil infiltration after UVR.
source: Conversely, topical COX-2 inhibition prevented fibroblast depletion and neutrophil infiltration after UVR.
evidence: This is supported by Ly6G staining quantification after celecoxib treatment.

claim: Loss of papillary fibroblasts is primarily induced by a deregulated inflammatory response.
source: We conclude that loss of papillary fibroblasts is primarily induced by a deregulated inflammatory response, with infiltrating T cells supporting fibroblast survival upon UVR-induced environmental stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of T cell depletion and COX-2 inhibition experiments.

claim: Infiltrating T cells support fibroblast survival upon UVR-induced environmental stress.
source: We conclude that loss of papillary fibroblasts is primarily induced by a deregulated inflammatory response, with infiltrating T cells supporting fibroblast survival upon UVR-induced environmental stress.
evidence: This is inferred from T cell depletion experiments showing increased fibroblast loss.

claim: UVR is essential for vitamin D synthesis.
source: While UVR is essential for vitamin D synthesis, prolonged (chronic) UVR exposure contributes to the development of skin cancer (photo-carcinogenesis) and accelerates ageing (photoageing) (Debacq-Chainiaux et al., 2012; Bernard et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Prolonged (chronic) UVR exposure contributes to the development of skin cancer (photo-carcinogenesis).
source: While UVR is essential for vitamin D synthesis, prolonged (chronic) UVR exposure contributes to the development of skin cancer (photo-carcinogenesis) and accelerates ageing (photoageing) (Debacq-Chainiaux et al., 2012; Bernard et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Prolonged (chronic) UVR exposure accelerates ageing (photoageing).
source: While UVR is essential for vitamin D synthesis, prolonged (chronic) UVR exposure contributes to the development of skin cancer (photo-carcinogenesis) and accelerates ageing (photoageing) (Debacq-Chainiaux et al., 2012; Bernard et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: UVC is absorbed by stratospheric ozone.
source: UVC is absorbed by stratospheric ozone while UVA and UVB penetrate the skin.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about UV radiation.

claim: UVA and UVB penetrate the skin.
source: UVC is absorbed by stratospheric ozone while UVA and UVB penetrate the skin.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about UV radiation.

claim: Chronic UVR damages the DNA, lipids, and proteins of skin cells directly (photochemical reactions) or indirectly via inflammation, reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, and matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) secretion.
source: Chronic UVR damages the DNA, lipids, and proteins of skin cells directly (photochemical reactions) or indirectly via inflammation, reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, and matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) secretion (Bernard et al., 2019; Naylor et al., 2011; Watson et al., 2014; Shih et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The dermis comprises distinct layers known as the papillary, reticular, and dermal white adipose tissue (DWAT) layers.
source: The connective tissue of the skin, the dermis, comprises distinct layers known as the papillary, reticular, and dermal white adipose tissue (DWAT) layers (Driskell et al., 2013; Rinkevich et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: During mouse skin development, multipotent fibroblasts differentiate into distinct subpopulations (lineages) that form the different layers.
source: During mouse skin development, multipotent fibroblasts differentiate into distinct subpopulations (lineages) that form the different layers.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Papillary fibroblasts beneath the basement membrane have an active Wnt signalling signature and are required for hair follicle formation.
source: While papillary fibroblasts beneath the basement membrane have an active Wnt signalling signature and are required for hair follicle formation, fibroblasts in the reticular dermal layer express high levels of genes associated with extracellular matrix (ECM) and immune signalling and mediate the initial phase of wound repair (Driskell et al., 2013; Rognoni et al., 2016; Philippeos et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Fibroblasts in the reticular dermal layer express high levels of genes associated with extracellular matrix (ECM) and immune signalling.
source: While papillary fibroblasts beneath the basement membrane have an active Wnt signalling signature and are required for hair follicle formation, fibroblasts in the reticular dermal layer express high levels of genes associated with extracellular matrix (ECM) and immune signalling and mediate the initial phase of wound repair (Driskell et al., 2013; Rognoni et al., 2016; Philippeos et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Fibroblasts in the reticular dermal layer mediate the initial phase of wound repair.
source: While papillary fibroblasts beneath the basement membrane have an active Wnt signalling signature and are required for hair follicle formation, fibroblasts in the reticular dermal layer express high levels of genes associated with extracellular matrix (ECM) and immune signalling and mediate the initial phase of wound repair (Driskell et al., 2013; Rognoni et al., 2016; Philippeos et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Within the first week of postnatal life, there is a coordinated switch in fibroblast behaviour from proliferative to quiescent, which is governed by ECM deposition/remodelling.
source: Within the first week of postnatal life, there is a coordinated switch in fibroblast behaviour from proliferative to quiescent, which is governed by ECM deposition/remodelling (Rognoni et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: UVB penetrates the epidermis and papillary dermis.
source: UVB penetrates the epidermis and papillary dermis, while UVA affects the full thickness of the dermis, including the subcutaneous fat (Watson et al., 2014; Barnes et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: UVA affects the full thickness of the dermis, including the subcutaneous fat.
source: UVB penetrates the epidermis and papillary dermis, while UVA affects the full thickness of the dermis, including the subcutaneous fat (Watson et al., 2014; Barnes et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Photoaged dermis is characterised by a loss of fibroblast density.
source: Photoaged dermis is characterised by a loss of fibroblast density and changes in ECM organisation, including depletion of fibrillin-rich microfibers in the papillary dermis and accumulation of elastin-rich elastic fibres in the reticular dermis, which are mediated, at least in part, by MMP activity (Naylor et al., 2011; Watson et al., 2014; Wlaschek et al., 2001; Scharffetter-Kochanek et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Photoaged dermis is characterised by depletion of fibrillin-rich microfibers in the papillary dermis.
source: Photoaged dermis is characterised by a loss of fibroblast density and changes in ECM organisation, including depletion of fibrillin-rich microfibers in the papillary dermis and accumulation of elastin-rich elastic fibres in the reticular dermis, which are mediated, at least in part, by MMP activity (Naylor et al., 2011; Watson et al., 2014; Wlaschek et al., 2001; Scharffetter-Kochanek et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Photoaged dermis is characterised by accumulation of elastin-rich elastic fibres in the reticular dermis.
source: Photoaged dermis is characterised by a loss of fibroblast density and changes in ECM organisation, including depletion of fibrillin-rich microfibers in the papillary dermis and accumulation of elastin-rich elastic fibres in the reticular dermis, which are mediated, at least in part, by MMP activity (Naylor et al., 2011; Watson et al., 2014; Wlaschek et al., 2001; Scharffetter-Kochanek et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Six healthy volunteers (two males, four females; mean age 44 ± 12 years) were recruited for the human UVB study.
source: For this study, six healthy volunteers (two males, four females; mean age 44 ± 12 years) were recruited.
evidence: This describes the study population.

claim: Buttock skin was exposed to three times the individual minimal erythema dose (MED) to induce a moderate sunburn reaction.
source: Their buttock skin was exposed to three times their individual minimal erythema dose (MED), sufficient to induce a moderate sunburn reaction characterised by histone H2AX phosphorylation (yH2AX), a central component of the DNA damage response and repair system, and cyclobutane pyrimidine dimer (CPD) accumulation in papillary fibroblasts (Barnes et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol with citation support.

claim: Three times MED UVB exposure is sufficient to induce histone H2AX phosphorylation (yH2AX) in papillary fibroblasts.
source: Their buttock skin was exposed to three times their individual minimal erythema dose (MED), sufficient to induce a moderate sunburn reaction characterised by histone H2AX phosphorylation (yH2AX), a central component of the DNA damage response and repair system, and cyclobutane pyrimidine dimer (CPD) accumulation in papillary fibroblasts (Barnes et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Three times MED UVB exposure is sufficient to induce cyclobutane pyrimidine dimer (CPD) accumulation in papillary fibroblasts.
source: Their buttock skin was exposed to three times their individual minimal erythema dose (MED), sufficient to induce a moderate sunburn reaction characterised by histone H2AX phosphorylation (yH2AX), a central component of the DNA damage response and repair system, and cyclobutane pyrimidine dimer (CPD) accumulation in papillary fibroblasts (Barnes et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: There was a loss of CD39/VM double-positive cells in the upper dermis of human skin following UVR exposure.
source: Quantifying and plotting fibroblast density changes over time in skin sections of individual healthy volunteers revealed a loss of CD39/VM double-positive cells in the upper dermis, which was followed by a transient increase in the repair phase before returning to pre-UVR treatment level within 2 weeks.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data from immunofluorescence staining.

claim: Loss of CD39/VM double-positive cells in human skin was followed by a transient increase in the repair phase before returning to pre-UVR treatment level within 2 weeks.
source: Quantifying and plotting fibroblast density changes over time in skin sections of individual healthy volunteers revealed a loss of CD39/VM double-positive cells in the upper dermis, which was followed by a transient increase in the repair phase before returning to pre-UVR treatment level within 2 weeks.
evidence: This is supported by time course quantification data.

claim: The acute UVR mouse model consisted of two consecutive UVB exposures (800 J/m2) separated by 2 days.
source: To uncover how different dermal fibroblast subpopulations are affected by UVB irradiation, we established an acute (ac)UVR mouse model consisting of two consecutive UVB exposures (800 J/m2) separated by 2 days, which induced moderate skin erythema – equivalent to a mild sunburn reaction in humans (Figure 1B; Shih et al., 2018; Thieden et al., 2005; Gyöngyösi et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol with citation support.

claim: The acute UVR mouse model induced moderate skin erythema equivalent to a mild sunburn reaction in humans.
source: To uncover how different dermal fibroblast subpopulations are affected by UVB irradiation, we established an acute (ac)UVR mouse model consisting of two consecutive UVB exposures (800 J/m2) separated by 2 days, which induced moderate skin erythema – equivalent to a mild sunburn reaction in humans (Figure 1B; Shih et al., 2018; Thieden et al., 2005; Gyöngyösi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Histology revealed epidermal hyperplasia 1 day after UVB exposure.
source: Histology revealed epidermal hyperplasia, UVB-induced angiogenesis, increased dermal immune cell infiltration, and temporary swelling of the papillary and reticular dermis at 1 day after UVB exposure (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in figures.

claim: Histology revealed UVB-induced angiogenesis 1 day after UVB exposure.
source: Histology revealed epidermal hyperplasia, UVB-induced angiogenesis, increased dermal immune cell infiltration, and temporary swelling of the papillary and reticular dermis at 1 day after UVB exposure (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in figures.

claim: Histology revealed increased dermal immune cell infiltration 1 day after UVB exposure.
source: Histology revealed epidermal hyperplasia, UVB-induced angiogenesis, increased dermal immune cell infiltration, and temporary swelling of the papillary and reticular dermis at 1 day after UVB exposure (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in figures.

claim: Histology revealed temporary swelling of the papillary and reticular dermis at 1 day after UVB exposure.
source: Histology revealed epidermal hyperplasia, UVB-induced angiogenesis, increased dermal immune cell infiltration, and temporary swelling of the papillary and reticular dermis at 1 day after UVB exposure (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in figures.

claim: There was a significant loss of upper dermal fibroblasts 1, 4, and 8 days after the second UVB exposure.
source: Quantification of PDGFRαH2BEGFP-positive cells showed a significant loss of upper dermal fibroblasts 1, 4, and 8 days after the second UVB exposure followed by a repair phase (Figure 1F), recapitulating the human in vivo findings (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of fibroblast density in mouse skin.

claim: The decrease in upper dermal fibroblasts correlated with an increase in DNA damage (yH2AX+) in dermal fibroblasts.
source: The decrease in upper dermal fibroblasts correlated with an increase in DNA damage, measured by the phosphorylation of histone H2AX (yH2AX+) (Figure 1C), and apoptosis (cCasp3+) in dermal fibroblasts, particularly in the papillary dermis, 1 and 4 days post-UVB (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by yH2AX immunofluorescence quantification.

claim: The decrease in upper dermal fibroblasts correlated with an increase in apoptosis (cCasp3+) in dermal fibroblasts, particularly in the papillary dermis, 1 and 4 days post-UVB.
source: The decrease in upper dermal fibroblasts correlated with an increase in DNA damage, measured by the phosphorylation of histone H2AX (yH2AX+) (Figure 1C), and apoptosis (cCasp3+) in dermal fibroblasts, particularly in the papillary dermis, 1 and 4 days post-UVB (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by cCasp3 immunofluorescence quantification.

claim: The number of immune cells (CD45+) increased markedly 1 day after irradiation and remained elevated for several days.
source: The number of immune cells (CD45+) increased markedly 1 day after irradiation and remained elevated for several days (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), accounting for the increase in total dermal cell density (DAPI+) during tissue repair (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by CD45 immunofluorescence quantification.

claim: Fibroblast proliferation increased at days 4 and 8, particularly in papillary fibroblasts, returning to normal thereafter.
source: Fibroblast proliferation increased at days 4 and 8, particularly in papillary fibroblasts, returning to normal thereafter (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by Ki67 immunofluorescence quantification.

claim: No αSma+ dermal fibroblasts were present after UVB exposure, indicating that UVB did not stimulate differentiation into myofibroblasts.
source: No αSma+ dermal fibroblasts were present, indicating that UVB did not stimulate differentiation into myofibroblasts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by αSma immunofluorescence staining.

claim: acUVB did not induce changes in the ECM that were detectable by collagen hybridising peptide (CHP) labelling.
source: We also noted that acUVB did not induce changes in the ECM that were detectable by collagen hybridising peptide (CHP) labelling, a molecular probe that recognises the triple helix structure of immature, damaged, and remodelling interstitial collagen fibres (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E; Hwang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by CHP staining analysis with citation.

claim: Gene Ontology analysis revealed that selected GO terms related to DNA damage, DNA repair, apoptosis, and cell stress were predominantly enriched in papillary fibroblasts in neonatal skin.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) analysis of differentially expressed genes between neonatal fibroblast subpopulations revealed that selected GO terms related to DNA damage, DNA repair, apoptosis, and cell stress were predominantly enriched in papillary fibroblasts, whereas expression of genes associated with GO term 'response to UV' or 'cellular response to UV' was not significantly increased in any fibroblast subpopulation at both time points (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and D).
evidence: This is based on reanalysis of published single-cell RNA-seq data.

claim: Expression of genes associated with GO term 'response to UV' or 'cellular response to UV' was not significantly increased in any fibroblast subpopulation in neonatal or adult mouse skin.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) analysis of differentially expressed genes between neonatal fibroblast subpopulations revealed that selected GO terms related to DNA damage, DNA repair, apoptosis, and cell stress were predominantly enriched in papillary fibroblasts, whereas expression of genes associated with GO term 'response to UV' or 'cellular response to UV' was not significantly increased in any fibroblast subpopulation at both time points (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and D).
evidence: This is based on reanalysis of published single-cell RNA-seq data.

claim: The enrichment of selected GO terms in papillary fibroblasts is due to their highly proliferative state in neonatal skin.
source: Indeed, the enrichment of selected GO terms in papillary fibroblasts is due to their highly proliferative state in neonatal skin (Rognoni et al., 2018; Phan et al., 2020), rather than indicating a different susceptibility/response to UV damage.
evidence: This is inferred from the data with citation support.

claim: Transcriptomic analysis of human sun-exposed eyelid skin revealed that no significant GO term enrichment was associated with response to UVR or cell stress in identified fibroblast subpopulations.
source: Similarly, transcriptomic analysis of human sun-exposed eyelid skin (Zou et al., 2021) and microdissected breast skin (Philippeos et al., 2018) revealed that no significant GO term enrichment was associated with response to UVR or cell stress in identified fibroblast subpopulations or in the upper and lower dermis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–G).
evidence: This is based on analysis of published transcriptomic data.

claim: Between different fibroblast subpopulations there are only minimal intrinsic differences in UV response, DNA damage/repair, and response to cell stress.
source: Our transcriptomic and GO term analysis suggests that between different fibroblast subpopulations there are only minimal intrinsic differences in UV response, DNA damage/repair, and response to cell stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the transcriptomic analysis results.

claim: The chronic UVR model consisted of 800 J/m2 UVB exposure twice a week for 8 weeks.
source: To test the impact of chronic UVR exposure on dermal fibroblasts, we established a chronic (ch)UVR model consisting of 800 J/m2 UVB exposure twice a week for 8 weeks.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: The chronic UVB treatment regime in C57BL/6 mice is rather mild compared to other recent studies.
source: This chronic UVB treatment regime in C57BL/6 mice is rather mild compared to other recent studies (Bald et al., 2014; Dai et al., 2007; Ohkumo et al., 2006; Han et al., 2017; Meeran et al., 2009; Kunisada et al., 2005) and induces a prominent tanning response (melanin deposition) in UVR-exposed back skin without disrupting the epidermal barrier (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to cited studies and experimental observations.

claim: Chronic UVB induces a prominent tanning response (melanin deposition) in UVR-exposed back skin without disrupting the epidermal barrier.
source: This chronic UVB treatment regime in C57BL/6 mice is rather mild compared to other recent studies (Bald et al., 2014; Dai et al., 2007; Ohkumo et al., 2006; Han et al., 2017; Meeran et al., 2009; Kunisada et al., 2005) and induces a prominent tanning response (melanin deposition) in UVR-exposed back skin without disrupting the epidermal barrier (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in figures.

claim: The moderate thickening of the epidermis after chronic UVB correlated with an increase in Ki67-positive keratinocytes.
source: The moderate thickening of the epidermis correlated with an increase in Ki67-positive keratinocytes (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by Ki67 immunofluorescence quantification.

claim: There was no significant difference between control and chUVB-exposed dermis in terms of proliferation (Ki67+ fibroblasts) 3 days after the final UVB treatment.
source: When the skin was examined 3 days after the final UVB treatment, there was no significant difference between control and chUVB-exposed dermis in terms of proliferation (Ki67+ fibroblasts) or apoptosis (cCasp3+ fibroblasts) (Figure 2B and C) and no αSma-positive interfollicular fibroblasts were detected (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Ki67 immunofluorescence quantification.

claim: There was no significant difference between control and chUVB-exposed dermis in terms of apoptosis (cCasp3+ fibroblasts) 3 days after the final UVB treatment.
source: When the skin was examined 3 days after the final UVB treatment, there was no significant difference between control and chUVB-exposed dermis in terms of proliferation (Ki67+ fibroblasts) or apoptosis (cCasp3+ fibroblasts) (Figure 2B and C) and no αSma-positive interfollicular fibroblasts were detected (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by cCasp3 immunofluorescence quantification.

claim: No αSma-positive interfollicular fibroblasts were detected after chronic UVB.
source: When the skin was examined 3 days after the final UVB treatment, there was no significant difference between control and chUVB-exposed dermis in terms of proliferation (Ki67+ fibroblasts) or apoptosis (cCasp3+ fibroblasts) (Figure 2B and C) and no αSma-positive interfollicular fibroblasts were detected (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by αSma immunofluorescence staining.

claim: There was an increased abundance of CD45-positive cells in the upper and lower dermis after chronic UVB.
source: However, there was an increased abundance of CD45-positive cells in the upper and lower dermis and an increase in blood vessels (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by CD45 immunofluorescence quantification.

claim: There was an increase in blood vessels after chronic UVB.
source: However, there was an increased abundance of CD45-positive cells in the upper and lower dermis and an increase in blood vessels (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by CD31 immunofluorescence staining.

claim: The ECM in chronically UVB-exposed skin was highly remodelled.
source: As observed in photoaged skin (Watson et al., 2014), the ECM in chronically UVB-exposed skin was highly remodelled (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is supported by Herovici staining and CHP labeling with citation.

claim: Herovici staining revealed accumulation of light blue-stained immature collagen, particularly beneath the basement membrane following chronic UVR.
source: Herovici staining revealed accumulation of light blue-stained immature collagen, particularly beneath the basement membrane following UVR; in contrast, mature collagen in control skin stained pink/purple (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by Herovici staining analysis.

claim: chUVR-treated skin showed significantly increased CHP staining, indicating that collagen fibres were damaged or actively remodelled.
source: In addition, chUVR-treated skin showed significantly increased CHP staining, indicating that collagen fibres were damaged or actively remodelled (Figure 2F; Hwang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by CHP staining quantification with citation.

claim: chUVR induced significant DNA damage in the epidermis and dermal fibroblasts, which was observed 1 day after the final UVB exposure.
source: chUVR induced significant DNA damage in the epidermis and dermal fibroblasts, which was observed 1 day after the final UVB exposure. The damage was progressively repaired post-UVR exposure, as measured by staining for yH2AX+ cells (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by yH2AX immunofluorescence quantification.

claim: DNA damage was progressively repaired post-UVR exposure, as measured by staining for yH2AX+ cells.
source: chUVR induced significant DNA damage in the epidermis and dermal fibroblasts, which was observed 1 day after the final UVB exposure. The damage was progressively repaired post-UVR exposure, as measured by staining for yH2AX+ cells (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by time course yH2AX immunofluorescence quantification.

claim: Fibroblast cell density was significantly decreased in the upper dermis after the final dose of chronic UVR and was not restored to control levels even after 30 days.
source: Quantification of fibroblasts (PDGFRαH2BEGFP+) in the upper and lower dermis showed that cell density was significantly decreased in the upper dermis after the final dose of UVR and was not restored to control levels even after 30 days (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of fibroblast density over time.

claim: chUVR did not affect the density of fibroblasts in the lower dermis.
source: In contrast, chUVR did not affect the density of fibroblasts in the lower dermis.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of fibroblast density.

claim: Total dermal cell density (DAPI+) transiently increased at 3 days post-chronic UVR, probably due to infiltrating immune cells.
source: Total dermal cell density (DAPI+) transiently increased at 3 days post-UVR, probably due to infiltrating immune cells (Figure 2D and I).
evidence: This is supported by DAPI quantification and inferred from immune cell data.

claim: Papillary fibroblasts can be specifically labelled with Lrig1-CreER when Cre-mediated recombination is induced at postnatal day 0 (P0).
source: Papillary fibroblasts can be specifically labelled with Lrig1-CreER, while Dlk1-CreER marks fibroblasts in the lower dermis when Cre-mediated recombination is induced at postnatal day 0 (P0) (Driskell et al., 2013; Rognoni et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Dlk1-CreER marks fibroblasts in the lower dermis when Cre-mediated recombination is induced at postnatal day 0 (P0).
source: Papillary fibroblasts can be specifically labelled with Lrig1-CreER, while Dlk1-CreER marks fibroblasts in the lower dermis when Cre-mediated recombination is induced at postnatal day 0 (P0) (Driskell et al., 2013; Rognoni et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: acUVR exposure of labelled transgenics confirmed the loss of papillary fibroblasts in the upper dermis.
source: acUVR exposure of labelled transgenics confirmed the loss of papillary fibroblasts in the upper dermis, whereas Dlk1-CreER-labelled cells in the lower dermis were not affected (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing experiments.

claim: Dlk1-CreER-labelled cells in the lower dermis were not affected by acUVR exposure.
source: acUVR exposure of labelled transgenics confirmed the loss of papillary fibroblasts in the upper dermis, whereas Dlk1-CreER-labelled cells in the lower dermis were not affected (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing experiments.

claim: At 4 days post-UVR, papillary lineage dermal cells started to repopulate the upper dermis.
source: At 4 days post-UVR, papillary lineage dermal cells started to repopulate the upper dermis. However, the density of cells was significantly reduced compared to control dermis (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing quantification.

claim: The density of papillary lineage cells at 4 days post-UVR was significantly reduced compared to control dermis.
source: At 4 days post-UVR, papillary lineage dermal cells started to repopulate the upper dermis. However, the density of cells was significantly reduced compared to control dermis (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing quantification.

claim: There were no detectable changes in the arrector pili muscle, dermal sheath, and dermal papilla fibroblasts of hair follicles upon acUVR treatment.
source: There were no detectable changes in the arrector pili muscle, dermal sheath, and dermal papilla fibroblasts of hair follicles upon acUVR treatment (Figure 3B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that these fibroblasts did not contribute to the repair of the damaged dermis (Rognoni et al., 2016; Kaushal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing analysis with citation.

claim: Hair follicle-associated fibroblasts did not contribute to the repair of the damaged dermis after acUVR.
source: There were no detectable changes in the arrector pili muscle, dermal sheath, and dermal papilla fibroblasts of hair follicles upon acUVR treatment (Figure 3B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that these fibroblasts did not contribute to the repair of the damaged dermis (Rognoni et al., 2016; Kaushal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from lineage tracing data with citation support.

claim: Dlk1-CreER-labelled cells of the reticular dermis did not expand or contribute to tissue repair after chronic UVR exposure.
source: As in the case of acUVR exposure, Dlk1-CreER-labelled cells of the reticular dermis did not expand or contribute to tissue repair (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing experiments.

claim: Lrig1-CreER-labelled cells were significantly reduced in the upper and lower dermis after chronic UVR and showed a patchy distribution.
source: Lrig1-CreER-labelled cells were significantly reduced in the upper and lower dermis and showed a patchy distribution.
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing quantification.

claim: Papillary fibroblast shapes were significantly elongated in chronic UVR skin, in contrast to acute UVR exposure.
source: Closer examination of papillary fibroblasts in chUVR skin revealed that, in contrast to acUVR exposure, their shapes were significantly elongated, suggesting that increased membrane protrusions may compensate for the fibroblast loss, as previously observed in aged skin (Marsh et al., 2018; Figure 3E and F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by cell elongation measurements with citation.

claim: Increased membrane protrusions may compensate for the fibroblast loss in chronic UVR skin, as previously observed in aged skin.
source: Closer examination of papillary fibroblasts in chUVR skin revealed that, in contrast to acUVR exposure, their shapes were significantly elongated, suggesting that increased membrane protrusions may compensate for the fibroblast loss, as previously observed in aged skin (Marsh et al., 2018; Figure 3E and F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from cell elongation data with citation support.

claim: Upon acUVR the upper dermis was replenished by papillary fibroblasts.
source: We conclude that upon acUVR the upper dermis was replenished by papillary fibroblasts.
evidence: This is concluded from lineage tracing experiments.

claim: Papillary fibroblasts in chUVR-treated skin were not replenished and instead changed shape, increasing their cell membrane protrusions.
source: In contrast, papillary fibroblasts in chUVR-treated skin were not replenished and instead changed shape, increasing their cell membrane protrusions (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is concluded from lineage tracing and cell elongation measurements.

claim: The lower dermal lineage was unaffected by acute or chronic UVR.
source: The lower dermal lineage was unaffected by acute or chronic UVR.
evidence: This is concluded from lineage tracing experiments.

claim: Most fibroblasts in untreated adult skin maintained positional stability and showed minimal displacement over time.
source: In agreement with previous measurements (Rognoni et al., 2018; Marsh et al., 2018), most fibroblasts in untreated adult skin maintained positional stability and showed minimal displacement over time (observed in three out of three imaged biological replicates) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo live imaging data with citations.

claim: At 1 day post-acUVB, only single papillary fibroblasts were observed moving into the deeper dermis or within the horizontal plane.
source: At 1 day post-acUVB, for example, we could only find single papillary fibroblasts moving into the deeper dermis or within the horizontal plane (Figure 4B, top panel, Figure 4—video 2).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo live imaging observations.

claim: Fibroblasts were slightly more motile along the (z) axis 1 day post-irradiation compared to control skin.
source: Quantification of cell displacement in the horizontal and vertical directions indicated that fibroblasts were slightly more motile along the (z) axis 1 day post-irradiation compared to control skin (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of cell displacement from live imaging.

claim: Most fibroblasts displayed minimal displacement and the direction of the observed movement appeared heterogenous at 1 day post-UVR.
source: However, most fibroblasts displayed minimal displacement and the direction of the observed movement appeared heterogenous (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of cell displacement from live imaging.

claim: At 4 days after UVR exposure, more fibroblasts showed increased random cell displacement within the horizontal and vertical dermal plane across the imaged dermis.
source: At 4 days after UVR exposure, more fibroblasts showed increased random cell displacement within the horizontal and vertical dermal plane across the imaged dermis (Figure 4B and C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, Figure 4—video 3).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of cell displacement from live imaging.

claim: The average mean displacement speed of fibroblasts was more heterogenous at 1 day post-UVR compared to control skin and increased significantly at 4 days post-UVR.
source: Consistent with this, the average mean displacement speed of fibroblasts was more heterogenous at 1 day post-UVR compared to control skin and increased significantly at 4 days post-UVR (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of cell velocity from live imaging.

claim: Fibroblasts with increased motility were present throughout the upper dermis at 4 days after UVR.
source: Plotting the individual cell mean speed across the upper dermis revealed that fibroblasts with increased motility were present throughout the upper dermis at 4 days after UVR (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by spatial analysis of cell velocity from live imaging.

claim: Fibroblast depletion in the papillary layer in the early UVR response is not associated with cell migration.
source: We conclude that fibroblast depletion in the papillary layer in the early UVR response is not associated with cell migration, whereas at 4 days post-acUVR fibroblasts become more motile, which correlates with ECM remodelling and fibroblast redistribution (Figure 3B and G).
evidence: This is concluded from live imaging data.

claim: At 4 days post-acUVR fibroblasts become more motile, which correlates with ECM remodelling and fibroblast redistribution.
source: We conclude that fibroblast depletion in the papillary layer in the early UVR response is not associated with cell migration, whereas at 4 days post-acUVR fibroblasts become more motile, which correlates with ECM remodelling and fibroblast redistribution (Figure 3B and G).
evidence: This is concluded from live imaging and lineage tracing data.

claim: The lack of directional migration indicates that fibroblast replenishment of the papillary dermis after UVR damage is a stochastic process similar to the fibroblast redistribution observed during dermal maturation and ageing.
source: The lack of directional migration indicates that fibroblast replenishment of the papillary dermis after UVR damage is a stochastic process similar to the fibroblast redistribution observed during dermal maturation and ageing (Rognoni et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from live imaging data with citation support.

claim: Epidermal Wnt signalling is a potent regulator of fibroblast behaviour during skin development and wound healing.
source: Epidermal Wnt signalling is a potent regulator of fibroblast behaviour during skin development and wound healing (Driskell et al., 2013; Collins et al., 2011; Lichtenberger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin activity was highly induced in epidermal and dermal cells at 1 and 4 days post-acUVR.
source: Wnt/β-catenin activity was highly induced in epidermal and dermal cells at 1 and 4 days post-acUVR (Figure 5A), which coincided with fibroblast DNA damage repair and proliferation (Figure 1C and H).
evidence: This is supported by TOPEGFP reporter mouse data.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin activity induction coincided with fibroblast DNA damage repair and proliferation.
source: Wnt/β-catenin activity was highly induced in epidermal and dermal cells at 1 and 4 days post-acUVR (Figure 5A), which coincided with fibroblast DNA damage repair and proliferation (Figure 1C and H).
evidence: This is inferred from temporal correlation of the data.

claim: During tissue repair and fibrosis, Wnt signalling has been shown to cooperate with YAP/TAZ signalling at multiple levels.
source: During tissue repair and fibrosis, Wnt signalling has been shown to cooperate with YAP/TAZ signalling at multiple levels (Piersma et al., 2015; Rognoni and Walko, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Dermal fibroblasts of the papillary dermis and IFE keratinocytes displayed increased nuclear YAP localisation in acute and chronic UVR-exposed skin.
source: Consistent with this, dermal fibroblasts of the papillary dermis and IFE keratinocytes displayed increased nuclear YAP localisation in acute and chronic UVR-exposed skin (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by YAP immunofluorescence quantification.

claim: Fibroblasts predominantly proliferated and expanded around existing and ectopic hair follicles in the lower dermis after epidermal β-catenin stabilisation and acUVR.
source: Analysing fibroblast distribution 8 days post-UVR and epidermal β-catenin stabilisation in PDGFRαH2BEGFP × Krt14ΔNβ-cat transgenics revealed that fibroblasts predominantly proliferated and expanded around existing and ectopic hair follicles in the lower dermis (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of transgenic mice.

claim: Increased abundance of fibroblasts after epidermal β-catenin stabilisation failed to efficiently repopulate the interfollicular dermis beneath the basement membrane.
source: However, this increased abundance of fibroblasts failed to efficiently repopulate the interfollicular dermis beneath the basement membrane and failed to restore fibroblast homeostasis and organisation in the papillary dermis.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of transgenic mice.

claim: Increased abundance of fibroblasts after epidermal β-catenin stabilisation failed to restore fibroblast homeostasis and organisation in the papillary dermis.
source: However, this increased abundance of fibroblasts failed to efficiently repopulate the interfollicular dermis beneath the basement membrane and failed to restore fibroblast homeostasis and organisation in the papillary dermis.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of transgenic mice.

claim: Wnt signalling is activated by UVR in the upper and lower dermis.
source: In conclusion, although Wnt signalling is activated by UVR in the upper and lower dermis, increasing fibroblast proliferation by genetically stabilising epidermal β-catenin was not sufficient to improve fibroblast regeneration of the papillary dermis.
evidence: This is concluded from TOPEGFP reporter data.

claim: Increasing fibroblast proliferation by genetically stabilising epidermal β-catenin was not sufficient to improve fibroblast regeneration of the papillary dermis.
source: In conclusion, although Wnt signalling is activated by UVR in the upper and lower dermis, increasing fibroblast proliferation by genetically stabilising epidermal β-catenin was not sufficient to improve fibroblast regeneration of the papillary dermis.
evidence: This is concluded from transgenic mouse experiments.

claim: Neutrophils are the first immune cell type to infiltrate into the dermal region after UVB exposure.
source: Neutrophils are the first immune cell type to infiltrate into the dermal region after UVB exposure (Savage et al., 1993; Katiyar et al., 1999), and this is followed by an influx of different T cell populations (Bernard et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Neutrophil infiltration is followed by an influx of different T cell populations after UVB exposure.
source: Neutrophils are the first immune cell type to infiltrate into the dermal region after UVB exposure (Savage et al., 1993; Katiyar et al., 1999), and this is followed by an influx of different T cell populations (Bernard et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The number of neutrophils increased in skin 1 day post-UVR.
source: The number of neutrophils increased in skin 1 day post-UVR (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data.

claim: There was an increase in the abundance, proliferation, and activation of different T cell populations, specifically CD8+ cytotoxic T cells and FoxP3+ regulatory T cells (Tregs) at 5 days post-UVR.
source: This was followed by an increase in the abundance, proliferation, and activation of different T cell populations, specifically CD8+ cytotoxic T cells and FoxP3+ regulatory T cells (Tregs) at 5 days post-UVR.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data.

claim: CD3+ T cells were depleted in the epidermis and increased in the dermis after UVR exposure.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis and quantification of CD3, CD8, and FoxP3 labelling revealed that CD3+ T cells were depleted in the epidermis and increased in the dermis (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantification.

claim: Cytotoxic T cells (CD8+) that are enriched in the lower dermis in control skin were significantly increased in the upper dermis after UVR exposure.
source: Cytotoxic T cells (CD8+) that are enriched in the lower dermis in control skin were significantly increased in the upper dermis after UVR exposure (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantification.

claim: Tregs (FoxP3+) that are closely associated with hair follicles in homeostasis significantly increased and expanded throughout the dermis at 3 days after acUVB exposure.
source: Similarly, Tregs (FoxP3+) that are closely associated with hair follicles in homeostasis (Ali et al., 2017) significantly increased and expanded throughout the dermis at 3 days after acUVB exposure (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantification with citation.

claim: The observed immune cell behaviour in mouse skin is consistent with that in human skin upon UVB exposure where neutrophil infiltration is followed by an increase in accumulation, activation, and proliferation of different T cell populations.
source: This is consistent with the observed immune cell behaviour in human skin upon UVB exposure where neutrophil infiltration is followed by an increase in accumulation, activation, and proliferation of different T cell populations (Hawkshaw et al., 2020; Rijken et al., 2006; Rhodes et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to human studies.

claim: Depletion of CD4- and CD8-positive cells significantly increased the loss of upper (papillary) fibroblasts after acUVR.
source: Depletion of either CD8+ or CD4+ cells significantly increased the loss of upper (papillary) fibroblasts (Figure 6E and F) and was associated with a significant increase in DNA damage (yH2AX + fibroblasts) and apoptosis (cCasp3+ fibroblasts) (Figure 6G and H) as well as a reduction in fibroblast proliferation (Ki67+) in the upper dermis but not in epidermal keratinocytes (Figure 6I, Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by antibody depletion experiments.

claim: CD4 or CD8 cell depletion was associated with a significant increase in DNA damage (yH2AX + fibroblasts) after acUVR.
source: Depletion of either CD8+ or CD4+ cells significantly increased the loss of upper (papillary) fibroblasts (Figure 6E and F) and was associated with a significant increase in DNA damage (yH2AX + fibroblasts) and apoptosis (cCasp3+ fibroblasts) (Figure 6G and H) as well as a reduction in fibroblast proliferation (Ki67+) in the upper dermis but not in epidermal keratinocytes (Figure 6I, Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by antibody depletion experiments.

claim: CD4 or CD8 cell depletion was associated with a significant increase in apoptosis (cCasp3+ fibroblasts) after acUVR.
source: Depletion of either CD8+ or CD4+ cells significantly increased the loss of upper (papillary) fibroblasts (Figure 6E and F) and was associated with a significant increase in DNA damage (yH2AX + fibroblasts) and apoptosis (cCasp3+ fibroblasts) (Figure 6G and H) as well as a reduction in fibroblast proliferation (Ki67+) in the upper dermis but not in epidermal keratinocytes (Figure 6I, Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by antibody depletion experiments.

claim: CD4 or CD8 cell depletion was associated with a reduction in fibroblast proliferation (Ki67+) in the upper dermis but not in epidermal keratinocytes after acUVR.
source: Depletion of either CD8+ or CD4+ cells significantly increased the loss of upper (papillary) fibroblasts (Figure 6E and F) and was associated with a significant increase in DNA damage (yH2AX + fibroblasts) and apoptosis (cCasp3+ fibroblasts) (Figure 6G and H) as well as a reduction in fibroblast proliferation (Ki67+) in the upper dermis but not in epidermal keratinocytes (Figure 6I, Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by antibody depletion experiments.

claim: Total dermal cells (DAPI+) in the lower dermis were significantly increased after CD4 or CD8 cell depletion and acUVR.
source: Although total dermal cells (DAPI+) in the lower dermis were significantly increased, PDGFRαH2BEGFP-positive cells were unchanged in the reticular dermal layer (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by DAPI quantification.

claim: PDGFRαH2BEGFP-positive cells were unchanged in the reticular dermal layer after CD4 or CD8 cell depletion and acUVR.
source: Although total dermal cells (DAPI+) in the lower dermis were significantly increased, PDGFRαH2BEGFP-positive cells were unchanged in the reticular dermal layer (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by fibroblast density quantification.

claim: αCD4 or αCD8 antibody treatment had no effect on fibroblasts in non-UVB-exposed skin.
source: In contrast, αCD4 or αCD8 antibody treatment had no effect on fibroblasts in non-UVB-exposed skin and injections of antibodies against IgG did not change the acute UVR skin response (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H–K).
evidence: This is supported by control experiments.

claim: Injections of antibodies against IgG did not change the acute UVR skin response.
source: In contrast, αCD4 or αCD8 antibody treatment had no effect on fibroblasts in non-UVB-exposed skin and injections of antibodies against IgG did not change the acute UVR skin response (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H–K).
evidence: This is supported by control experiments.

claim: acUVB exposure leads to an infiltration of neutrophils that is followed by an increase and redistribution of different T cell subpopulations in the dermis.
source: In summary, we observe that acUVB exposure leads to an infiltration of neutrophils that is followed by an increase and redistribution of different T cell subpopulations in the dermis.
evidence: This is concluded from immunofluorescence and flow cytometry data.

claim: Depletion of CD4- and CD8-positive cells significantly impairs fibroblast survival and regeneration in the upper dermis after acUVB exposure by increasing DNA damage, apoptosis, and reducing fibroblast proliferation.
source: Depletion of CD4- and CD8-positive cells significantly impairs fibroblast survival and regeneration in the upper dermis after acUVB exposure by increasing DNA damage, apoptosis, and reducing fibroblast proliferation.
evidence: This is concluded from antibody depletion experiments.

claim: CD4+ T cell depletion significantly increases and prolongs the acute UVB-induced cutaneous inflammatory response.
source: Previous reports have suggested that CD4+ T cell depletion significantly increases and prolongs the acute UVB-induced cutaneous inflammatory response (Hatton et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Acute UVR exposure induced the release of pro-inflammatory prostaglandins, including prostaglandin E2 (PGE-2) in the skin.
source: Acute UVR exposure induced the release of pro-inflammatory prostaglandins, including prostaglandin E2 (PGE-2) in the skin, which was further increased after CD4+ and CD8+ cell depletion (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is supported by PGE-2 measurements.

claim: PGE-2 levels were further increased after CD4+ and CD8+ cell depletion following acute UVR.
source: Acute UVR exposure induced the release of pro-inflammatory prostaglandins, including prostaglandin E2 (PGE-2) in the skin, which was further increased after CD4+ and CD8+ cell depletion (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is supported by PGE-2 measurements.

claim: Cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) is a key enzyme for prostaglandin synthesis and can be induced in multiple cell types in response to pro-inflammatory stimuli.
source: Cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) is a key enzyme for prostaglandin synthesis and can be induced in multiple cell types in response to pro-inflammatory stimuli (Williams et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: COX-2 expression was significantly increased in the epidermis and dermis, including fibroblasts, at 1 day post-acUVB before returning to baseline 4 days after UVR exposure.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis and quantification revealed that COX-2 expression was significantly increased in the epidermis and dermis, including fibroblasts, at 1 day post-acUVB before returning to baseline 4 days after UVR exposure (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by COX-2 immunofluorescence quantification.

claim: Inhibition of COX-2 following UVB irradiation has been shown to inhibit several parameters of UVR-induced acute inflammation, including vascular permeability, infiltration of neutrophils, PGE-2 production, as well as acute oxidative damage.
source: Inhibition of COX-2 following UVB irradiation has been shown to inhibit several parameters of UVR-induced acute inflammation, including vascular permeability, infiltration of neutrophils, PGE-2 production, as well as acute oxidative damage (Wilgus et al., 2003; Wilgus et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: COX-2 inhibition significantly inhibited fibroblast depletion in the upper dermis after UVR treatment.
source: Notably, COX-2 inhibition significantly inhibited fibroblast depletion in the upper dermis and neutrophil infiltration (Ly6G+) after UVR treatment (Figure 7E–G).
evidence: This is supported by celecoxib treatment experiments.

claim: COX-2 inhibition significantly inhibited neutrophil infiltration (Ly6G+) after UVR treatment.
source: Notably, COX-2 inhibition significantly inhibited fibroblast depletion in the upper dermis and neutrophil infiltration (Ly6G+) after UVR treatment (Figure 7E–G).
evidence: This is supported by celecoxib treatment experiments.

claim: DNA damage in dermal fibroblasts (yH2AX+) was reduced by COX-2 inhibition after UVR.
source: Furthermore, DNA damage in dermal fibroblasts (yH2AX+) was reduced (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is supported by yH2AX quantification after celecoxib treatment.

claim: Celecoxib treatment did not affect fibroblast proliferation (Ki67+) after acute UVR exposure.
source: In contrast, celecoxib treatment did not affect fibroblast proliferation (Ki67+) and total dermal cell density (DAPI+) after acute UVR exposure (Figure 7I and J).
evidence: This is supported by Ki67 quantification after celecoxib treatment.

claim: Celecoxib treatment did not affect total dermal cell density (DAPI+) after acute UVR exposure.
source: In contrast, celecoxib treatment did not affect fibroblast proliferation (Ki67+) and total dermal cell density (DAPI+) after acute UVR exposure (Figure 7I and J).
evidence: This is supported by DAPI quantification after celecoxib treatment.

claim: PGE-2 has been recently shown to increase fibroblast apoptosis through E prostanoid (EP)2 and EP4 receptor signalling, resulting in activation of phosphatase and tensin homologue on chromosome 10 (PTEN) and downstream inhibition of protein kinase B /AKT.
source: Besides inhibiting fibroblast proliferation, collagen synthesis, migration, and differentiation into myofibroblasts, PGE-2 has been recently shown to increase fibroblast apoptosis through E prostanoid (EP)2 and EP4 receptor signalling, resulting in activation of phosphatase and tensin homologue on chromosome 10 (PTEN) and downstream inhibition of protein kinase B /AKT, an important pro-survival signal (Huang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: EP4 is the major EP receptor in skin.
source: EP4 is the major EP receptor in skin (Regard et al., 2008) and is expressed by dermal fibroblasts (Joost et al., 2020; Sennett et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: EP4 is expressed by dermal fibroblasts.
source: EP4 is the major EP receptor in skin (Regard et al., 2008) and is expressed by dermal fibroblasts (Joost et al., 2020; Sennett et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: EP4 was strongly increased in the epidermis and dermis and remained elevated in the upper dermis up to 14 days post-UVR in mouse skin.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis and quantification of EP4 showed that EP4 was strongly increased in the epidermis and dermis and remained elevated in the upper dermis up to 14 days post-UVR (Figure 7K).
evidence: This is supported by EP4 immunofluorescence quantification.

claim: EP4 expression was significantly increased in the epidermis and dermis at 1 and 4 days after acUVB exposure before returning to lower levels after 7 days in human skin.
source: In line with this, immunostaining skin sections for EP4 in the UVB-treated human skin time course revealed that EP4 expression was significantly increased in the epidermis and dermis at 1 and 4 days after acUVB exposure before returning to lower levels after 7 days in both skin compartments (Figure 7L).
evidence: This is supported by EP4 immunostaining quantification in human skin.

claim: The UVB-induced increase in PGE-2 level and EP4 expression influences the dermal fibroblast UVB damage response and survival.
source: These findings suggest that the UVB-induced increase in PGE-2 level and EP4 expression influences the dermal fibroblast UVB damage response and survival (Figure 7M).
evidence: This is inferred from the combined PGE-2 and EP4 data.

claim: The loss of fibroblasts in the upper dermis is primarily induced by an UVR-induced inflammatory response involving PGE-2 and EP4 signalling that can be supressed by COX-2 inhibition.
source: In summary, we have shown that the loss of fibroblasts in the upper dermis is primarily induced by an UVR-induced inflammatory response involving PGE-2 and EP4 signalling that can be supressed by COX-2 inhibition.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined experimental results.

claim: Infiltrating/activated T cells support fibroblast survival and regeneration following UVR-induced environmental stress by controlling the inflammatory response to UVR exposure.
source: Our data suggest that infiltrating/activated T cells support fibroblast survival and regeneration following UVR-induced environmental stress by controlling the inflammatory response to UVR exposure (Figure 7M).
evidence: This is inferred from T cell depletion and COX-2 inhibition experiments.

claim: Loss of papillary fibroblasts is primarily due to apoptosis rather than movement of papillary fibroblasts into the deeper dermis.
source: Our immunofluorescence, lineage tracing, and in vivo live imaging results showed that the loss of papillary fibroblasts is primarily due to apoptosis rather than movement of papillary fibroblasts into the deeper dermis.
evidence: This is concluded from multiple experimental approaches.

claim: After acute UVR fibroblasts start proliferating, increase motility and restore tissue density.
source: After acute UVR fibroblasts start proliferating, increase motility and restore tissue density.
evidence: This is concluded from proliferation and live imaging data.

claim: Prolonged exposure to UVR prevented repopulation of fibroblasts in the upper dermis even after 30 days post-UVR.
source: In contrast, prolonged exposure to UVR prevented repopulation of fibroblasts in the upper dermis even after 30 days post-UVR (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by long-term quantification of fibroblast density.

claim: Previous studies of chronic UVB irradiation reported a reduced cell density in the papillary dermis even 200 days after final UVB exposure.
source: These observations are in line with previous studies of chronic UVB irradiation that reported a reduced cell density in the papillary dermis even 200 days after final UVB exposure (Dai et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Loss of the papillary lineage is associated with premature skin ageing, reduced regeneration, and a profibrotic environment.
source: Loss of the papillary lineage is associated with premature skin ageing, reduced regeneration, and a profibrotic environment (Driskell et al., 2013; Rognoni et al., 2016; Phan et al., 2020; Lichtenberger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Both full thickness wounds and UVR-induced tissue damage induce a pronounced inflammatory response and activation of Wnt/β-catenin and YAP/TAZ signalling in the epidermis and dermis.
source: While both forms of tissue damage induce a pronounced inflammatory response and activation of Wnt/β-catenin and YAP/TAZ signalling in the epidermis and dermis, UVR-induced tissue damage is repaired with minimal fibroblast proliferation, migration, and myofibroblast differentiation.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of the data.

claim: UVR-induced tissue damage is repaired with minimal fibroblast proliferation, migration, and myofibroblast differentiation.
source: While both forms of tissue damage induce a pronounced inflammatory response and activation of Wnt/β-catenin and YAP/TAZ signalling in the epidermis and dermis, UVR-induced tissue damage is repaired with minimal fibroblast proliferation, migration, and myofibroblast differentiation.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental data.

claim: ECM is a potent regulator of fibroblast behaviour and inhibits proliferation during skin development and regeneration.
source: We recently showed that ECM is a potent regulator of fibroblast behaviour and inhibits proliferation during skin development and regeneration (Rognoni et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The inhibitory signal of the ECM can be partly overcome by overexpression of epidermal β-catenin, which induces the expression of several fibroblast growth factors.
source: The inhibitory signal of the ECM can be partly overcome by overexpression of epidermal β-catenin, which induces the expression of several fibroblast growth factors (Lichtenberger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: During skin homeostasis most dermal fibroblasts are stationary, yet active random fibroblast migration has been observed close to growing hair follicles where the surrounding ECM is extensively remodelled.
source: In support of this concept, during skin homeostasis most dermal fibroblasts are stationary, yet active random fibroblast migration has been observed close to growing hair follicles where the surrounding ECM is extensively remodelled (Marsh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Upon full-thickness wounding, fibroblasts start migrating towards the wound where they randomly distribute and expand during the early wound repair phase.
source: In contrast, upon full-thickness wounding, we and others have shown that fibroblasts start migrating towards the wound where they randomly distribute and expand during the early wound repair phase (Rognoni et al., 2018; Jiang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: During wound healing, chemoattractants such as platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) are key regulators of fibroblast chemotaxis.
source: During wound healing, chemoattractants such as platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) are key regulators of fibroblast chemotaxis (Melvin et al., 2011); however, the intrinsic and extrinsic signals controlling fibroblast migration after UVR exposure remain unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The intrinsic and extrinsic signals controlling fibroblast migration after UVR exposure remain unclear.
source: During wound healing, chemoattractants such as platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) are key regulators of fibroblast chemotaxis (Melvin et al., 2011); however, the intrinsic and extrinsic signals controlling fibroblast migration after UVR exposure remain unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Recent laser or genetic ablation experiments have revealed that loss of dermal fibroblasts is repaired through a mixture of proliferation/migration and reorganisation of the plasma membrane network.
source: Recent laser or genetic ablation experiments have revealed that loss of dermal fibroblasts is repaired through a mixture of proliferation/migration and reorganisation of the plasma membrane network (Marsh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: A similar mechanism of fibroblast repair (proliferation/migration and membrane reorganisation) may apply during repair of UVR-induced tissue damage.
source: Our data indicate that a similar mechanism may apply during repair of UVR-induced tissue damage.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data.

claim: The progressive loss of fibroblasts during skin ageing is balanced by increasing membrane protrusions rather than fibroblast proliferation or migration.
source: This is in line with the observation of Marsh et al. that the progressive loss of fibroblasts during skin ageing is balanced by increasing membrane protrusions rather than fibroblast proliferation or migration (Marsh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Repeated UVB tissue damage accelerates the process of fibroblast loss and membrane protrusion increase observed in ageing.
source: Our data indicate that repeated UVB tissue damage accelerates this process (photoageing).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of chronic UVR data with ageing.

claim: Resident immune cells are essential for skin barrier function, pathogen defence, and wound healing.
source: Resident immune cells are not only essential for skin barrier function, pathogen defence, and wound healing but also provide essential signals for hair follicle growth and skin regeneration (Gay et al., 2013; Ali et al., 2017; Nosbaum et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Resident immune cells provide essential signals for hair follicle growth and skin regeneration.
source: Resident immune cells are not only essential for skin barrier function, pathogen defence, and wound healing but also provide essential signals for hair follicle growth and skin regeneration (Gay et al., 2013; Ali et al., 2017; Nosbaum et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: This study identifies an additional function of resident immune cells: promoting the survival of dermal fibroblasts during environmental stress.
source: Here we identify an additional function, that of promoting the survival of dermal fibroblasts during environmental stress.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental results.

claim: Neutrophil-derived reactive oxidants are potent mediators of UVB-induced tissue damage and tumorigenesis because of their cytotoxicity and immunosuppression.
source: Neutrophil-derived reactive oxidants are potent mediators of UVB-induced tissue damage and tumorigenesis because of their cytotoxicity and immunosuppression (Savage et al., 1993; Katiyar et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Tregs are suggested to inhibit the UVR-induced inflammatory response.
source: This was followed by infiltration of different types of T cells; in particular, Tregs became highly activated and proliferative (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), which is suggested to inhibit the UVR-induced inflammatory response (Bernard et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Treg expansion throughout the interfollicular dermis upon UVR exposure could potentially promote an immunosuppressive environment.
source: While in homeostatic conditions Tregs are predominantly located around hair follicles (Ali et al., 2017), their expansion throughout the interfollicular dermis was evident upon UVR exposure, and this could potentially promote an immunosuppressive environment.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed Treg distribution.

claim: Whether there is direct cross-talk between T cells and dermal fibroblasts during the UVR tissue damage response is currently unclear.
source: Whether there is also direct cross-talk between T cells and dermal fibroblasts during the UVR tissue damage response is currently unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: A recent study in human skin has identified CD4+ GATA3+ and CD8+ GATA3+ T cells as the predominant T cell populations in UVR-induced inflammation.
source: A recent study in human skin has identified CD4+ GATA3+ and CD8+ GATA3+ T cells as the predominant T cell populations in UVR-induced inflammation, and these are therefore likely to contribute to tissue resolution via dermal communication (Hawkshaw et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: CD4+ GATA3+ and CD8+ GATA3+ T cells are likely to contribute to tissue resolution via dermal communication.
source: A recent study in human skin has identified CD4+ GATA3+ and CD8+ GATA3+ T cells as the predominant T cell populations in UVR-induced inflammation, and these are therefore likely to contribute to tissue resolution via dermal communication (Hawkshaw et al., 2020).
evidence: This is inferred from cited work.

claim: Production of multiple pro-inflammatory prostaglandins, including PGE-2, is promoted following UVR as a result of arachidonic acid release by phospholipases and by induction of COX-2 expression in various skin cells.
source: Production of multiple pro-inflammatory prostaglandins, including PGE-2, is promoted following UVR as a result of arachidonic acid release by phospholipases and by induction of COX-2 expression in various skin cells (Rhodes et al., 2009; Fuller, 2019; Athar et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Following acUVB exposure of human skin pro-inflammatory prostaglandins including PGE-2 peak at 24 hr before normalising after 4 days.
source: In line with our mouse data, it has been reported that following acUVB exposure of human skin pro-inflammatory prostaglandins including PGE-2 peak at 24 hr before normalising after 4 days (Hawkshaw et al., 2020; Rhodes et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: PGE-2 governs diverse biological functions that are mediated by signalling through four distinct E-type prostanoid (EP) receptors, EP1–4.
source: PGE-2 governs diverse biological functions that are mediated by signalling through four distinct E-type prostanoid (EP) receptors, EP1–4 (Konya et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: EP4 is a Gs-coupled receptor regulating cAMP/PKA, MEK/ERK1/2, NF-ƙB, and PI3K/ERK/Akt signalling; these pathways are important for cell survival, proliferation, migration, differentiation, angiogenesis, and inflammation.
source: The major EP receptor in skin is EP4, which is a Gs-coupled receptor regulating cAMP/PKA, MEK/ERK1/2, NF-ƙB, and PI3K/ERK/Akt signalling; these pathways are important for cell survival, proliferation, migration, differentiation, angiogenesis, and inflammation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about EP4 receptor signalling.

claim: In fibroblasts, PGE-2 binding to EP4 has been shown to increase PTEN activity and Fas expression and decrease survivin expression, thereby promoting apoptosis.
source: In fibroblasts, PGE-2 binding to EP4 has been shown to increase PTEN activity and Fas expression and decrease survivin expression, thereby promoting apoptosis (Huang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The increased PGE-2 levels and EP4 expression in the dermis in the early UVR response coincide with the observed fibroblast depletion at 1 and 4 days after UVB exposure.
source: In line with these observations, the increased PGE-2 levels and EP4 expression in the dermis in the early UVR response coincide with the observed fibroblast depletion at 1 and 4 days after UVB exposure (Figure 7M).
evidence: This is inferred from temporal correlation of the data.

claim: The COX enzyme inhibitor aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) efficiently protects keratinocytes and melanocytes from acute UVB-induced DNA damage by decreasing cutaneous inflammation and PGE-2 levels in skin.
source: This is consistent with the observation that the COX enzyme inhibitor aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) efficiently protects keratinocytes and melanocytes from acute UVB-induced DNA damage by decreasing cutaneous inflammation and PGE-2 levels in skin (Rahman et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: Aspirin may enhance dermal fibroblast survival and regeneration upon UVR-induced environmental stress.
source: Based on our findings, aspirin may also enhance dermal fibroblast survival and regeneration upon UVR-induced environmental stress.
evidence: This is speculated based on the experimental findings.

claim: Whether the anti-inflammatory activities of aspirin could help prevent fibroblast-associated changes in photoaged skin warrants investigation in the future.
source: Whether the anti-inflammatory activities of aspirin could help prevent fibroblast-associated changes in photoaged skin warrants investigation in the future.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Specific inhibition of COX-2 reduces dermal fibroblast loss which may have therapeutic applications in the treatment of UVR-induced skin damages and photoageing.
source: Specific inhibition of COX-2 reduces dermal fibroblast loss which may have therapeutic applications in the treatment of UVR-induced skin damages and photoageing.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental results with speculation about therapeutic applications.

claim: Fibroblast senescence is linked to age-associated cancer risk.
source: Our findings could also be relevant to stromal changes in skin cancer, in which fibroblast senescence is linked to age-associated cancer risk (Lewis et al., 2010; Procopio et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.
